tracks.title: The Stardust Engine
tracks.loreNote: This alternate version of "The Stardust Engine" was one of the original demos shopped around to record companies when the band formed in 1986. Apex Records signed them but rejected this version, burying the final studio version as track 13 on 1987's *Electric Color*. The band famously despises Apex for what happened to them during the 1992 label dispute. For this vault release, they officially retitled this early cut "(The Rejected Mix)" instead of naming Apex Records directly, serving as a quiet nod to their lingering resentment.

tracks.title: Midnight Drivers
tracks.loreNote: This is an early, raw basement recording of what would eventually become the title track of their 2001 retro-engineered album. Recorded in 1987 before the track was polished in the studio (which Apex Records ultimately deemed too dark and shelved), this gritty demo captures the isolating, moody energy the band originally envisioned before the label interference.

tracks.title: Radio Silence
tracks.loreNote: A 1986 deep cut demo that Apex Records threw out during the *Electric Color* selection process because it was deemed "too heavy on the synths and too light on the pop". It remained a fan-favorite myth among diehards who traded bootleg cassette tapes, finally getting an official release on this vault compilation.

tracks.title: Empty Arenas
tracks.loreNote: Recorded in late 1990 shortly after Ryan's life-altering bus accident, this solemn, stripped-down acoustic demo (`Empty Arenas (Early Demo)`) reflects the band's raw fear that they would never be able to play live again. Deemed too bleak for the *Friction* sessions, the tape remained locked in the vault until *Lost Sounds* (2007)—though fourteen years after cutting this sketch, the band resurrected the song during the 2004 *Progress Street* sessions and transformed it into a thunderous, full-band 1980s Album-Oriented Rock (AOR) stadium anthem with polished lyrics and a full drum kit.

tracks.title: The Contract
tracks.loreNote: The legendary 1992 punk-rock vent track. Recorded entirely in secret during their bitter legal dispute with Apex Records, the band absolutely shreds their former label for their suffocating creative control. The sheer anger in Ryan's guitar work makes this a standout deep cut. It was never intended for public release, serving strictly as a therapeutic middle finger to the studio executives.

tracks.title: Neon Hearts
tracks.loreNote: This is the raw, acoustic sketch of what would become their heavily manufactured 1989 hit, "Neon Hearts." Without the glossy, heavy studio synths imposed by Apex Records, this early draft reveals the song to be a surprisingly tender, intimate ballad rather than a club-ready pop anthem.

tracks.title: Sanctuary: Zero G
tracks.loreNote: An early demo outtake of the massive closer from the 2003 *Sanctuary: Zero-G* album. Before it was expanded into a 74-minute symphonic journey with a spoken-word planetarium outro, it existed as this raw, atmospheric space-rock demo. It showcases the core duet between Ryan and Cassidy and the foundation of The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound® before the studio gloss and orchestral layers were applied.

tracks.title: Steel and Synthetics
tracks.loreNote: Originally written during the 1997 *Hard Reset* sessions. It serves as a love letter to the band's dual identities—the "Steel" of rock and the "Synthetics" of electronic music. It was cut simply due to runtime constraints on the double album, but remains a fan favorite.

tracks.title: Our Own Frequency
tracks.loreNote: A brand new track recorded specifically for the 2007 *Lost Sounds* compilation, intentionally designed to simulate the stripped-down, acoustic music Ryan and Cassidy were making together back in 1985 (before their cousins Evan and Tyler joined to form The Stardust Engine). After digging through years of painful, heavily-manufactured Apex Records history, they wanted to close the album by returning to their roots. Written and recorded in a single afternoon with just an acoustic guitar and a piano, "Our Own Frequency" is a triumphant, intimate declaration of their bond as brother and sister. It is the exact kind of acoustic scratch track they always wanted to make, completely free of label interference.

tracks.title: Atmosphere
tracks.loreNote: Recorded in September 1992 for the canceled *Friction* album, this early rough cut sounds distinctly like an early-1990s demo—and the band was never happy with it. Four years after including this raw archival cut on *Lost Sounds*, Cassidy and Ryan finally recorded the definitive, finalized studio version of *"Atmosphere"* on 2011's *Starfield Calibration*, using **The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™** to bring the song back to the 1980s sound they loved so much.

tracks.title: Ignition: The Forger's Call
tracks.loreNote: The legendary October 1986 4-track Tascam Portastudio cassette demo recorded inside the unheated garage at 412 Progress Street NE in Blacksburg, Virginia—submitted by five college kids (Ryan O'Connell, Cassidy O'Connell, Evan Wright, Tyler Wright, and 16-year-old dual-enrolled Holly O'Connell) to the CPI Student Government Association contest to replace the football team's entrance march. Protected by 16-year-old Holly's historic $1.00 Perpetual Mutual Cross-License ('The Progress Street Redline'), this raw 1986 cassette cut features the mechanical click of Holly's 4-track tape deck, Tyler Wright striking a salvaged automobile brake drum on the concrete garage floor with a sledgehammer (TING... BOOM!), Cassidy's raw Oberheim OB-Xa analog synth brass, Ryan's overdriven garage-metal guitar riff, and Cassidy, Evan, and Tyler shouting the gang-vocal (IGNITION!) response into a single shared Shure SM57 microphone.
